detailed_rationale:
Union Bank of India's Q1 FY27 print (reported 15-Jul-2026) continued a genuinely improving asset-quality arc: net profit of Rs 5,332 crore (+29.5% YoY from Rs 4,116 crore), NII of Rs 10,037 crore (+10.1% YoY), and NIM recovering sequentially to 2.76-2.80% from 2.64% in Q4 FY26 (helped by an 18bps cut in deposit cost) but still short of management's own >3% target and below FY25's 2.91% average - the rate-cut transmission cycle is a real headwind. GNPA fell to 2.65% (from 2.82% QoQ and 3.60% YoY) and NNPA to 0.47%, with PCR at a strong 95.05%. Credit cost dropped to just 38bps (-9bps YoY) and the slippage ratio to 82bps (from 99bps a year ago) - this looks like a durable improvement, not a one-quarter flattering number, but it is running near cyclical lows for the book.

The growth mix carries the main watch items. Loan growth of 12.5% YoY is outrunning total deposit growth of just 3.5% YoY (CASA deposits alone grew a healthier 11.72%, and CASA ratio sits near 35%), the classic PSU-bank funding-gap pattern seen across the system this cycle - a name to watch if wholesale funding costs rise. ROA held at 1.36% for three straight quarters and ROE at 17.23%, both strong for a PSU bank, but roughly a third of the YoY profit delta is a provisioning base effect: total provisions fell 41.5% YoY (Rs 1,667 crore to Rs 975 crore), versus ~15.8% growth in core operating profit - so the headline PAT growth is not purely organic. More pointed: recoveries declined quarter-on-quarter even as slippages held near lows, and SMA-2 (61-90 day overdue) accounts rose Rs 850 crore, concentrated in MSME - an early-stage stress signal that, if it migrates to NPA, would reverse the improving-ratio narrative the stock is currently being credited for. Capital is comfortable (CRAR 18.46%, CET1 16.38%), and the board-approved Rs 8,000-10,000 crore raise (~Rs 3,000 crore equity via QIP/rights + Rs 5,000 crore+ AT1/Tier-2 bonds, approved June 2026) reads as precautionary Basel-cushion building for growth, not a distress signal - but it is a real EPS/BVPS dilution overhang for minority holders whenever priced. A minor RBI penalty of Rs 95.4 lakh (March 2026, asset-classification/unauthorized-transaction lapses) is routine and not a governance red flag; there is no CEO-succession or board-crisis binary stacking here of the kind we flagged on HDFCBANK.

On reverse-DCF: the stock trades near book (P/B ~1.0x, P/E ~7x at Rs 169.8, market cap ~Rs 1.32 lakh crore). A 17.23% reported ROE against 1.0x P/B looks statistically cheap on the surface, but that ROE is inflated by a credit-cost/recovery tailwind that is unlikely to persist - 38bps credit cost is well below a realistic through-cycle PSU-bank run-rate of 70-100bps, and NIM is still running 20-30bps below management's own target under the current rate cycle. Normalizing both gets to a through-cycle ROE closer to 12-13%, which at a reasonable PSU-bank cost of equity (~13-14%, reflecting execution/governance discount) and ~7-8% nominal growth justifies a P/B band of roughly 0.9-1.1x - i.e., the market is pricing this business about right on a normalized basis, not offering a margin of safety, but also not obviously rich.
recommendation_rationale: Hold, not Sell: the core franchise metrics (asset quality, capital adequacy, ROA trajectory) are genuinely improving and six-plus quarters of credible execution argue against a bearish call. But it is not a name to add into either - the headline profit growth is partly a fading provisioning tailwind rather than fully organic, the SMA-2 build in MSME plus the QoQ recovery decline are live early-stage stress signals, the loan/deposit growth gap is a funding-quality concern, and the pending Rs 8,000-10,000 crore capital raise is a dilution overhang. With the stock already priced roughly for a normalized (not headline) ROE, there is no valuation cushion that would justify anything other than Hold, and no forensic breakdown (rushed write-backs, restructuring bulge, governance crisis) severe enough to justify Sell.
summary: Union Bank of India's asset quality keeps improving on the surface - gross NPAs down to 2.65% and net NPAs to 0.47% as of June 2026, with strong capital (18.46% CRAR) - and profitability metrics (17%+ ROE, 1.36% ROA) are good for a PSU bank. But a meaningful part of the recent profit jump comes from lower provisions rather than pure business improvement, deposits are growing much slower than loans, some early stress is showing up in small-business accounts, and a large capital raise is in the pipeline that will dilute existing shareholders. At roughly book value, the stock looks fairly priced for what it can sustainably deliver once these tailwinds fade - not expensive, but not offering a discount either. We rate it a Hold.
positive_para: Asset quality has genuinely improved, not just cosmetically: GNPA down from 3.60% to 2.65% over the past year, NNPA at a clean 0.47%, provision coverage at a strong 95.05%, and the slippage ratio nearly halved to 82bps. Credit costs are at multi-year lows (38bps) and capital is comfortable (CRAR 18.46%, CET1 16.38%) even before the planned raise. ROA has held at 1.36% for three consecutive quarters and ROE at 17.23%, both strong for a PSU bank, with loan growth running at a healthy 12.5% YoY and CASA deposits growing 11.72%. The stock trades close to book value, which is not demanding for a bank posting these return ratios if they hold.
negative_para: The bear case starts with the quality of the earnings beat: roughly a third of the YoY profit growth came from a 41.5% drop in provisions rather than core business improvement, and 38bps credit cost is unsustainably low versus a realistic through-cycle PSU-bank run rate of 70-100bps - when it normalizes upward, so-far-strong ROA/ROE will compress. More concretely, recoveries fell quarter-on-quarter even as the bank was reporting improving ratios, and SMA-2 (early-warning stressed) accounts rose Rs 850 crore in the MSME book - exactly the kind of early-stage deterioration that PSU-bank asset-quality cycles have turned on before. Deposit growth of just 3.5% YoY against 12.5% loan growth is a funding-gap pattern that raises the cost/availability question for continued credit growth, and NIM at 2.76-2.80% remains structurally below management's own >3% target in a rate-cut cycle. Layer on a pending Rs 8,000-10,000 crore capital raise (partly equity) that will dilute existing per-share book value and earnings once priced, and this is a stock with real embedded risks behind an attractively-improving headline.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~1.0x P/B against a reported 17.23% ROE, the market would be underpricing the bank if that ROE were sustainable - but it isn't fully organic: credit costs (38bps) and the provisioning tailwind are running well below a realistic through-cycle level (70-100bps), and NIM remains 20-30bps short of management's own target. Normalizing for both points to a through-cycle ROE closer to 12-13%, which at a PSU-bank cost of equity of ~13-14% and ~7-8% nominal growth justifies almost exactly the current 0.9-1.1x P/B band. Conclusion: fairly valued on a normalized basis, not cheap once the write-back/low-credit-cost tailwind is stripped out.

technical_commentary: Strong, intact multi-year uptrend with higher highs confirmed as recently as Feb-2026 (fresh ATH) and a fully bullish, well-separated MA stack (price>10m>20m>40m). The Mar-2026 single-month -19% break was sharp but has since stabilized into a steady, low-volatility grind higher (Rs159 to Rs169 over four months) rather than a breakdown, with 2026 volume expanding alongside the push to new highs -- demand-side, not distribution.
